articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1 Million Mystery: Where Did the ARPA Funds Go?
articles.dek: Federal pandemic relief money earmarked for small business recovery remains unspent or unaccounted for as the September deadline looms. County administrators won't say why.
brief: $2.1 million in American Rescue Plan Act funds designated for Escambia County small business recovery remains unaccounted for with a September 2026 federal deadline approaching.
County Administrator Wes Moreno and finance staff have declined multiple interview requests and have not responded to public records requests filed in April.
At least three small business owners say their approved grant applications from 2023 were never funded despite receiving confirmation letters.
articles.body:
The office smells like fryer grease and frustration. Maria Delgado stands behind the counter of her Nine Mile Road taqueria, smoothing a crumpled letter dated November 2023. The Escambia County seal sits at the top. Congratulations, it says. Your business has been approved for a $15,000 ARPA Small Business Recovery Grant.

She never saw a dime.

"I called them maybe twenty times," Delgado said. "They kept saying it was coming. Then they stopped answering."

Delgado is one of at least three Escambia County small business owners who received approval letters for grants funded by the American Rescue Plan Act but never received payment. Together, their approved amounts total $52,000. That's a fraction of a larger problem.

According to the county's own ARPA spending reports submitted to the U.S. Treasury Department, $2.1 million allocated for small business recovery assistance remains listed as "obligated but not expended" as of March 2026. The federal deadline to spend all ARPA funds is September 30, 2026. After that date, unspent money returns to the federal government.

County Administrator Wes Moreno has declined four interview requests from The Flightline over the past six weeks. His office has not responded to a public records request filed April 8 seeking documentation of all ARPA small business grants approved, disbursed, and pending.

Florida law requires responses to public records requests "within a reasonable time." Seventy-three days is not reasonable.

The Paper Trail Stops

The county commission approved the small business recovery program in August 2022, setting aside $4.5 million from Escambia's $64 million ARPA allocation. The program would provide grants of $10,000 to $25,000 to businesses with fewer than 50 employees that could demonstrate pandemic-related revenue losses.

County records show the program received 847 applications. Commission meeting minutes from 2023 reference "ongoing review" of applications but provide no specific numbers on approvals or disbursements.

The Flightline obtained copies of three approval letters through the business owners who received them. All three are dated between September and November 2023. All three include identical language: "Funds will be disbursed within 45 business days of this notice."

Tom Hensley owns a pressure washing company in Cantonment. His approval letter promised $12,000. "I budgeted around it," he said. "I was going to buy a new truck. I waited and waited. Finally gave up around summer 2024."

Hensley said he called the county finance office approximately a dozen times. "Different answers every time. Processing delays. Staff turnover. System upgrades. Always something."

The third business owner, who requested anonymity because she still has pending permit applications with the county, was approved for $25,000. She provided The Flightline with a copy of her approval letter and a log of 34 phone calls and emails to county offices between December 2023 and August 2024. None resulted in payment or a clear explanation.

Commission in the Dark

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said he was unaware of the disbursement issues until contacted by The Flightline.

"That's concerning," Bergosh said. "We approved that program in good faith. If there are approved applicants who haven't been paid, I want to know why."

Bergosh said he would request a briefing from the county administrator at the next commission meeting, scheduled for July 1.

Commissioner Lumon May did not respond to requests for comment. Commissioner Steven Barry's office said he was traveling and unavailable. Commissioners Mike Kohler and Brandi Stinson did not respond.

The commission has not discussed the small business recovery program in a public meeting since February 2024, according to a review of meeting minutes and agendas.

The Clock Runs Out

The September deadline creates urgency. Under Treasury Department rules, any ARPA funds not spent by September 30, 2026 must be returned. The county cannot request an extension.

If the $2.1 million remains unspent, it will revert to the federal government. The businesses approved for grants will receive nothing. The pandemic recovery purpose of the funds will go unfulfilled.

Other Florida counties have faced scrutiny over ARPA spending. In 2024, the state auditor flagged Santa Rosa County for inadequate documentation of $800,000 in small business grants, though that county ultimately spent its allocation before the deadline pressure mounted.

Escambia County has not faced a state audit of its ARPA spending. Whether one is forthcoming is unclear. The Florida Auditor General's office said county audit schedules are not public information until audits are announced.

Questions Without Answers

The Flightline submitted the following questions to County Administrator Moreno's office on April 8, again on May 15, and a third time on June 10:

How many small business recovery grant applications were approved?

How many approved grants have been disbursed, and what is the total amount?

Why were some approved applicants never paid?

What is the county's plan to spend or account for the remaining $2.1 million before September 30?

No response has been received to any submission.

The county's public information officer, Karla Weathersby, said in a brief phone call that "staff is working on the request" but could not provide a timeline. That was May 22.

Back on Nine Mile Road, Maria Delgado has stopped waiting. She took out a high-interest loan last year to replace her walk-in cooler. The monthly payments eat into her already thin margins.

"I don't understand how they can send you a letter saying yes, you're approved, and then just disappear," she said. "It's not right."

She still has the letter. She keeps it in a folder beneath the register, next to her business license and health inspection certificate. A reminder, she said, of what was promised.

The county has 102 days to provide an answer. Or the money goes back to Washington, and the question becomes permanent.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The 500-Unit Question: Who's Building Pensacola's Next Workforce Housing?
articles.dek: With NAS Pensacola expanding and downtown rents up 40% since 2022, developers are chasing density approvals while neighborhoods push back. A look at three projects reshaping the city's housing fight.
brief: Three major workforce housing developments totaling over 1,400 units are moving through Pensacola's approval process as military expansion drives demand
Downtown Pensacola rents have increased 40% since 2022, with average one-bedroom units now exceeding $1,600 monthly
Neighborhood opposition has delayed two projects by more than six months, raising questions about the city's ability to meet housing targets
articles.body:
The parking lot behind the old Brownsville Community Center sits empty on a Tuesday morning. Knee-high grass pushes through cracks in the asphalt. A faded sign advertises youth basketball registration for a program that ended three years ago.

By 2028, if Escambia County commissioners approve the pending rezoning application, this 12-acre site will hold 312 apartment units marketed to Navy personnel and base contractors. The developer, a Jacksonville-based firm called Coastal Workforce Partners, promises rents 15% below market rate for qualifying tenants.

It is one of three large-scale workforce housing projects currently navigating Pensacola's approval process. Together they represent more than 1,400 new units. Together they have drawn more than 600 public comments, overwhelmingly opposed.

The math is simple. The politics are not.

The Demand Side

NAS Pensacola added 2,100 personnel between 2023 and 2025 as the Navy consolidated training operations from bases in Mississippi and Texas. Another 800 are expected by early 2027. The base now employs more than 23,000 military and civilian workers, making it the largest single employer in Northwest Florida.

Those workers need housing. The base's own housing stock covers roughly 1,800 families. The waitlist, according to a Naval Facilities Engineering Command spokesperson, currently holds more than 400 names with an average wait time of 14 months.

"We're telling E-4s and E-5s with families to find something in the private market," said Chief Petty Officer Marcus Webb, who runs the base's housing referral office. "The private market isn't ready for them."

The numbers bear this out. According to rental data from Zillow and confirmed by local property managers, average asking rent for a one-bedroom apartment in downtown Pensacola hit $1,642 in May 2026. In May 2022, that figure was $1,173. A 40% increase in four years.

Two-bedroom units near the base—the East Hill, Brownsville, and West Pensacola neighborhoods—average $1,890 monthly. Basic Allowance for Housing for an E-5 with dependents stationed at NAS Pensacola is $1,827.

"The BAH doesn't cover rent anymore," Webb said. "That's a first in my 18 years here."

Three Projects, Three Fights

The Brownsville development is the furthest along. Coastal Workforce Partners purchased the community center site from the county in 2024 for $2.1 million. The company filed its rezoning application in September 2025, requesting a change from public/institutional use to high-density residential.

The project calls for four five-story buildings arranged around a central courtyard. Plans include a pool, fitness center, and dedicated parking structure. Coastal has committed to reserving 30% of units for tenants earning between 80% and 120% of area median income—the federal definition of workforce housing.

Neighbors have packed three public hearings. Their concerns center on traffic, specifically the intersection of W Street and Pace Boulevard, which already fails during morning rush hour according to Florida Department of Transportation metrics.

"You're putting 600 cars onto streets built for 200," said Denise Harmon, president of the Brownsville Neighborhood Association, at the most recent hearing in April. "Show me the traffic study that says this works."

Coastal's traffic study, submitted to the county, projects 487 additional daily vehicle trips. The study recommends a dedicated turn lane on Pace Boulevard and signal timing adjustments. FDOT has not yet commented on the proposal.

The commission delayed its vote in April. A new hearing is scheduled for July 15.

The second project sits three miles east, on a vacant lot behind Sacred Heart Hospital. Tampa-based Atticus Development Group wants to build 580 units there—a mix of studios, one-bedrooms, and two-bedrooms aimed at hospital workers and young professionals.

The site is already zoned for multi-family housing. What Atticus needs is a height variance. Current zoning caps buildings at four stories. Atticus wants seven.

"The economics don't work at four stories," said Grant Holloway, Atticus's regional development director, in a phone interview. "Construction costs are up 30% since 2020. Land costs are up more than that. You need density to make the rents affordable."

The company's pro forma, portions of which were shared with The Flightline, projects break-even rents of $1,480 for a one-bedroom at seven stories. At four stories, that figure rises to $1,720.

Sacred Heart has submitted a letter supporting the project, noting that 40% of its nursing staff commutes from outside Escambia County.

Neighbors in the adjacent Scenic Heights subdivision are less enthusiastic. A petition opposing the height variance has gathered more than 300 signatures. The Pensacola City Council will hear the variance request on August 3.

The third project hasn't reached public hearings yet, but it may prove the most contentious. Local developer Ray Sansom—no relation to the former state representative—has assembled 28 acres along Scenic Highway just north of I-10. He envisions a 540-unit mixed-use development with ground-floor retail and workforce housing above.

The catch: the site currently holds 23 single-family homes, all occupied. Sansom has acquired 19 of them through private sales. Four owners have refused to sell.

"This isn't eminent domain," Sansom said. "I'm offering fair market value plus 20%. But I can't force anyone."

The holdout owners, who declined to be named, have retained an attorney. No legal action has been filed. Sansom says he'll proceed with a modified site plan if necessary, though he acknowledges it would reduce the unit count significantly.

The Density Debate

Pensacola's comprehensive plan, last updated in 2019, calls for 3,500 new housing units in the urban core by 2030. According to city planning department records, approximately 1,100 have been permitted since then. Most are single-family homes in the northern suburbs.

"We're not building where people want to live," said City Council member Jennifer Brahney, whose district includes downtown and East Hill. "We're building where land is cheap and neighbors don't show up to meetings."

Brahney has proposed amendments to the city's land development code that would streamline approval for multi-family projects near transit corridors and major employers. The amendments would reduce parking minimums and allow administrative approval for projects meeting certain density and affordability thresholds.

The proposal has drawn opposition from several neighborhood associations and at least two of Brahney's colleagues on the council.

"Administrative approval means no public input," said Council member Casey Jones. "My constituents deserve a voice in what gets built next door."

Brahney's amendments are scheduled for first reading in September.

What Gets Built

Back at the Brownsville site, the grass keeps growing. The basketball hoops are gone now, removed by county work crews last month. The backboards had rusted through.

Marcus Webb, the housing officer at NAS Pensacola, drives past the site twice a day on his commute from Cantonment. He knows about the project, knows about the delays.

"I've got a sailor right now living in an extended-stay motel off Pine Forest Road," he said. "Family of four. Been there since February. They're on every waitlist I can find them."

He paused.

"People keep asking who's going to build the housing we need. I keep waiting for an answer."

The county commission meets July 15. The city council meets August 3. The grass keeps growing.

articles.label: Environment
articles.headline: Red Tide Returns to Pensacola Beach Earlier Than Expected
articles.dek: Marine scientists detected elevated Karenia brevis levels off Santa Rosa Island this week, months ahead of typical bloom season. Tourism officials are watching the water—and the forecast.
brief: Water samples collected Tuesday off Pensacola Beach showed Karenia brevis concentrations at medium levels, prompting a beach advisory from Escambia County officials.
The bloom arrived two to three months earlier than the typical late summer pattern, according to researchers at the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
Tourism industry representatives report no major cancellations yet but are monitoring conditions ahead of the July 4 holiday weekend.
articles.body:
The water off Casino Beach looked normal Wednesday morning. Families spread towels on the sand. Kids ran into the surf. A pod of dolphins worked the second sandbar, drawing pointed fingers from the pier.

What nobody could see was drifting a few miles offshore: a bloom of Karenia brevis, the microscopic algae that produces brevetoxins and turns Gulf waters the color of rust. By late afternoon, the first reports of respiratory irritation started coming in from beachgoers near Portofino.

"We're seeing medium concentrations in samples collected Tuesday," said Dr. Rachel Hendricks, a harmful algal bloom researcher with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. "That's above background levels but below what we'd classify as a high bloom. The concern is timing."

Red tide typically arrives along the Panhandle in late August or September, pushed inshore by prevailing winds after blooms develop in deeper Gulf waters. This year's detection in mid-June marks one of the earliest appearances in the Pensacola area in more than a decade.

Hendricks pointed to warmer-than-average water temperatures this spring and an unusually calm wind pattern that allowed the bloom to drift north from its likely origin point near Tampa Bay.

"We had 84-degree surface temps in early June," she said. "That's favorable for Karenia growth. Combine that with light southerly winds, and you get transport up the coast."

A tourism industry on alert

Escambia County issued a beach advisory Wednesday, recommending that people with chronic respiratory conditions avoid the shore until conditions improve. The advisory stops short of a closure—swimming remains permitted—but the yellow flags now flying at county access points carry an asterisk.

"We're being proactive with information," said county spokeswoman Maria Torres. "People should know what they're walking into."

For the tourism industry, the timing is precarious. Pensacola Beach hotels report strong bookings through July, with occupancy rates running 12% above the same period last year. The July 4 weekend typically marks the peak of summer season.

"Right now, we're not seeing cancellations," said Darien Schaefer, president of Visit Pensacola. "But we're watching this closely. A prolonged bloom could absolutely impact visitor decisions."

The last significant red tide event in the Pensacola area occurred in October 2018, when high concentrations of Karenia brevis killed thousands of fish along Santa Rosa Island and sent tourists fleeing from the sulfurous smell of decay. Local hotels reported a 23% drop in occupancy that month compared to the prior year.

What happens next

FWC researchers will continue sampling twice weekly at sites from Perdido Key to Navarre Beach. The bloom's trajectory depends largely on wind patterns over the coming days.

"If we get sustained offshore winds, this could disperse quickly," Hendricks said. "Onshore winds will concentrate it along the beaches. It's really a weather question at this point."

The National Weather Service forecast for Pensacola shows light and variable winds through the weekend, shifting to southwesterly flow early next week—a pattern that could push the bloom closer to shore.

For now, the beach remains open. The dolphins keep feeding. And somewhere past the breakers, a billion invisible cells drift with the current, waiting on the wind.
